meta.title: Time Machine — NVIDIA, $100 from IPO to today
meta.premise: $100 invested at NVIDIA's IPO price on January 22, 1999
meta.method: value = 4,000 split-adjusted shares x split-adjusted year-end close. Price return only: dividends, taxes and fees excluded.
sources: companiesmarketcap.com NVIDIA stock price history (annual % cross-check)
NVIDIA investor relations and newsroom (corporate events)

years.label: 1999 — IPO
years.summary: NVIDIA prices its IPO at $12 a share on the Nasdaq. $100 buys 8.33 shares — the position that six later stock splits turn into 4,000 shares.

years.event: GeForce 256 and the birth of the GPU
years.summary: In October NVIDIA launches GeForce 256 and markets it as the world's first GPU. The stock ends its first year at $46.94, nearly quadrupling from the IPO price.

years.event: Dot-com peak and the first stock split
years.summary: PC graphics demand stays strong and NVIDIA wins the graphics contract for Microsoft's first Xbox. The company splits its stock 2-for-1 in June, its first.

NVIDIA's best calendar year ever. GeForce3 ships, the Xbox launches with NVIDIA silicon inside, the company joins the S&P 500 and splits 2-for-1 again — all while the broader tech market is falling apart.

years.event: SEC accounting investigation and the Microsoft dispute
years.summary: The SEC and the U.S. Attorney's Office open an investigation into NVIDIA's accounting; the company restates results in April. A pricing dispute with Microsoft over Xbox chips and a broad semiconductor downturn compound it. The worst year in NVIDIA's history: down 82.8%.
NVIDIA reaches an agreement in principle with the SEC to resolve the restatement matter, technology markets recover, and the stock doubles off the bottom.
A quiet year. NVIDIA introduces SLI and rebuilds its position against ATI, but the stock finishes essentially where it started.
Demand for increasingly powerful PC graphics supports growth, and NVIDIA wins the graphics contract for Sony's PlayStation 3.

In November NVIDIA introduces CUDA alongside the GeForce 8800 GTX, letting ordinary programmers run general-purpose parallel workloads on a GPU. The public SDK follows in February 2007. This is the single most consequential decision in the company's history.
NVIDIA launches the Tesla line for high-performance computing and splits 3-for-2. Momentum carries right up to the edge of the financial crisis.

years.event: Global financial crisis and the bumpgate defect
years.summary: The financial crisis crushes consumer and technology demand. NVIDIA also takes a $200M+ charge for defective mobile GPU packaging. Down 76.3%, its second-worst year.
Markets recover sharply and NVIDIA rebounds with the semiconductor group, more than doubling.
The Fermi generation ships late, hot and power-hungry. The post-crisis rally fades and the stock gives back ground.
NVIDIA pushes into mobile with Tegra and buys baseband maker Icera, but investors reassess growth expectations and the stock drifts lower.
Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton train AlexNet on two GeForce GTX 580s and win ImageNet by a landslide. Deep learning becomes a GPU problem. The market notices none of it — the stock falls 11.5%.
Research labs standardise on CUDA for neural network training, laying the groundwork for the data-center business that does not exist yet.
The Maxwell architecture delivers a large jump in performance per watt, strengthening both gaming and professional computing.
Industry adoption of GPU-accelerated machine learning broadens sharply and NVIDIA begins to be valued as an AI company rather than a graphics vendor.
Pascal and the P100 arrive as AI adoption accelerates; NVIDIA hand-delivers the first DGX-1 to OpenAI. The best-performing stock in the S&P 500 that year, up 223.9%.
The V100 sets the standard for AI training while cryptocurrency miners buy every consumer GPU they can find. Three sources of demand at once.

years.event: Crypto crash and the inventory glut
years.summary: Mining demand collapses, leaving channel inventory NVIDIA had not accounted for. The stock falls 31%. In 2022 the SEC fines NVIDIA $5.5M for inadequate disclosure of how much of its 2018 gaming growth had come from crypto.
Gaming normalises and data-center demand takes over as the story. NVIDIA agrees to buy Mellanox for $6.9B in March.
The pandemic drives gaming and cloud demand, Ampere and the A100 launch, and the Mellanox acquisition closes on April 27 for $7.13B — giving NVIDIA the networking half of the AI data center.

AI, gaming, data center and networking all expand together and NVIDIA splits 4-for-1 in July. It now looks like a full accelerated-computing platform rather than a chip vendor. The Arm acquisition, however, is heading for collapse.

years.event: Rate shock, crypto collapse, first China controls
years.summary: Mining collapses, gaming inventory swells, rising rates compress growth multiples, the $40B Arm deal is abandoned, and in August the U.S. restricts A100 and H100 exports to China. The stock halves — five weeks before ChatGPT ships.
ChatGPT turns H100s into the scarcest industrial good on earth. The May earnings guidance beats consensus by roughly 50% and adds $184B of market value in a day. Up 238.9%.

years.event: Blackwell and the capex arms race
years.summary: Blackwell launches as hyperscalers commit to unprecedented AI infrastructure spending. NVIDIA joins the Dow and splits 10-for-1 in June — which changes accessibility, not value.

On January 27 DeepSeek's R1 wipes $589B off NVIDIA in one session — the largest single-day loss in market history. The company recovers to become the first ever worth $4T in July and $5T on October 29, then closes the year buying Groq's assets for about $20B. April's H20 export ban costs it a $4.5B charge.

years.event: Rubin, China at zero, Hugging Face
years.summary: A record close of $235.47 on May 14 is followed by a slide to $192.53 in June. Revenue is still compounding — $81.6B in the April quarter, up 85% — but China data-center revenue has fallen to effectively zero and Rubin faces supply delays. On September 3 NVIDIA agrees to buy Hugging Face for $12.93B.

eras.name: GPU computing
eras.note: AlexNet proves the GPU is a compute engine.

eras.name: AI infrastructure
eras.note: The world buys everything NVIDIA can build.

notes.caveat: Annual returns show the market's reaction around each period. They are not a causal measurement of the event itself — price moves for earnings, valuation, macro conditions and expectations simultaneously.
notes.precision: Values are computed from unadjusted year-end closes divided by the split factor still outstanding at that date, then multiplied by 4,000 shares. Deriving them instead from published two-decimal split-adjusted prices introduces errors up to 4% in the pre-2008 years, when the adjusted price was under $1.
